title: Governance & Audit
text: All money is in $M. Losses are expected loss per targeted ransomware campaign, and the model assumes one campaign per year. All values are illustrative.

title: Governance & Audit
section: How a board should use this
text:
How a board should use this
Use this analysis as a challenge to the budget, not as an allocation engine. The numbers are synthetic. What carries over to your own firm is the logic: attackers respond to what we defend, and the best plan is the one that still works when our read of the attacker is wrong.
A board can ask three things. Does our plan state who we think the attacker is? Has anyone tested the plan against a different attacker? What would we change if our threat intelligence were wrong by a third?

title: Governance & Audit
text:
Assumptions register


Code
reg |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(id = "ID", assumption = "Assumption", why_it_matters = "Why it matters",
             how_it_could_fail = "How it could fail", where_tested = "Where tested") |>
  gt_se() |>
  cols_align(align = "left")




Table 1: Assumptions behind the analysis, why each matters, how it could fail, and where it is tested.









ID
Assumption
Why it matters
How it could fail
Where tested




A1
One ransomware campaign per year
Loss figures are per campaign; the budget is annual
Several campaigns or repeat attacks would multiply loss and change the best trade-offs
Not tested (out of scope: repeated play)


A2
Single adversary type
The crew's payoffs drive every strategy
Different attackers (insiders; nation-states) want different assets
Not tested (out of scope: attacker mixtures)


A3
The crew observes coverage before choosing a target
Equilibrium logic relies on the attacker responding to what it sees
An attacker who cannot see defenses attacks closer to its prior
Partly tested through the noisy-crew sweep (Robustness page)


A4
Coverage cost is linear
Linear cost makes the allocation a clean budget split
Real controls show diminishing returns and fixed costs
Not tested


A5
Coverage acts as the probability an attack is stopped
Turns spending into loss reduction
Controls fail in correlated ways; coverage may not map to a probability
Not tested


A6
A stopped attack still costs 10% of the full loss
Sets the value of coverage for the defender
A higher share weakens the gain from coverage; a lower share strengthens it
Sensitivity table: 5% and 20% (robust still best)


A7
Every asset keeps at least 25% hygiene coverage
Fixes a minimum on every asset including low-value ones
A different floor changes how much budget is free to allocate
Sensitivity table: 15% and 35% (robust still best)


A8
Synthetic calibration
All asset values are illustrative
Real values could reorder the strategies
Misestimation Monte Carlo (Robustness page) stresses the crew's payoffs only


A9
Robust rationality parameter lambda = 2
Controls how noisy the robust strategy assumes the crew is
A very different crew would make a different lambda best
Chosen on a separate simulation seed; lambda sweep (Robustness page)


A10
Crew payoff error is lognormal with sigma 0.35
Defines how badly the firm may misjudge the crew
Larger or biased errors would hurt every strategy
Sensitivity table: sigma 0.20 and 0.50; seed-stability check (diagnostics)


A11
Assets fail independently (no lateral movement)
Each attack's loss depends only on the asset hit
Ransomware crews pivot through identity and corporate IT to reach other systems
Sensitivity table: higher identity and corporate IT losses (robust still best)











How to read the table. Each row is something we assumed to build the model. The columns say why the assumption matters, how it could turn out wrong, and where this site tests it, if anywhere.
What the table tells you. Several assumptions are not tested here. These are the first places to look when applying the approach to real data, because a wrong assumption can reorder the strategies.

Sensitivity
We changed one assumption at a time and reran the full comparison. The robust strategy was best in 8 of 8 cases, including a lateral-movement case where an identity or corporate IT breach spreads and costs more.

title: Governance & Audit
text:
Limitations
The model has no repeated play: one campaign, one decision. It has no deception or honeypots, which can change what the crew sees. It has one attacker type, so insiders and state actors are out of scope. Assets fail independently: a breach of identity or corporate IT does not spread to other systems, although real ransomware crews often move laterally. The sensitivity table tests a simple version of this. The budget is static, so it does not respond to new intelligence during the year.
Natural follow-ons are repeated play, mixtures of attacker types, and the attack-graph Markov chain project.

title: Governance & Audit
text:
Further reading
For a framework that tests any risk model, see Three Questions for Any Risk Model.

title: Allocating the Budget

The firm
The firm has 500 staff. Its cloud platform is critical infrastructure for its bank and broker clients. It has $9.0M a year to allocate across six assets. That budget includes a hygiene floor: every asset keeps at least 25% coverage, because compliance demands it.


Code
mu <- log(assets$L) - LOSS_SIGMA^2 / 2

    Asset = ASSET_SHORT[asset_id],

section: Where we and the crew disagree
text:
Where we and the crew disagree


Code
assets |>
  mutate(rank_L = rank(L), rank_V = rank(V), label = ASSET_SHORT[asset_id]) |>
  ggplot(aes(rank_L, rank_V)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, color = "#0166CC") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 4, box.padding = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.7, 6.3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, limits = c(0.7, 6.3)) +
  labs(x = "Rank by our loss (6 = largest)", y = "Rank by crew value (6 = most attractive)",
       title = "Our biggest worries are not the crew's favorites")








Figure 1: Rank of each asset by our loss against rank by the crew’s value. Distance from the diagonal measures disagreement.






How to read the plot. Each dot is an asset. Moving right means a larger loss for us; moving up means more attractive to the crew. The dashed diagonal marks assets where both sides agree on the ranking.
What the plot tells you. The pipeline is our largest loss but ranks last for the crew, so the crew has little reason to attack it. Identity is the reverse. A plan built only on our own risk ranking will misjudge where the crew goes.

title: Allocating the Budget
section: Four strategies at the base budget
text:
Four strategies at the base budget
We compare four ways to spend $9.0M. The robust strategy joins on page 4.


Code
four <- c("risk_ranked", "proportional", "uniform", "textbook")
base$strategies |>
  filter(strategy %in% four) |>
  left_join(sm |> select(strategy, target), by = "strategy") |>
  mutate(
    strategy = factor(STRAT_LABELS[strategy], levels = STRAT_LABELS[four]),
    asset = factor(ASSET_SHORT[asset_id], levels = ASSET_SHORT),
    hit = ifelse(asset_id == target, "Crew's target", "Other asset")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(asset, coverage, fill = hit)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~strategy, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Crew's target" = "#7A3E9D", "Other asset" = "#C8C8C8"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Coverage") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))








Figure 2: Coverage by asset under four strategies. The crew’s chosen target is highlighted in each panel.






How to read the plot. Each panel is one way to split the budget. Bars show how much of each asset is protected. The purple bar is the asset the crew would attack if it reads our defenses perfectly.
What the plot tells you. Risk-ranked piles protection onto two assets and leaves identity at the floor, which is where the crew goes. Proportional and uniform spread money out but still leave identity as the best target. Only the textbook plan changes the crew’s destination.

sm |>
  filter(strategy %in% four) |>
  transmute(Strategy = STRAT_LABELS[strategy], Target = ASSET_SHORT[target], Loss = loss_rational) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Target = "Crew target", Loss = "Expected loss ($M)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = Loss, decimals = 1) |>
  gt_se()

title: Allocating the Budget
text:
Interpretation
Risk-ranked funds the platform and pipeline and leaves identity at the floor. The crew sees this and goes to identity, for an expected loss of $13.9M.
The textbook equilibrium does something cleverer. It sets coverage so that the crew earns the same on 5 of the six assets. It lets the attack fall on corporate IT, a low-impact target, and cuts expected loss to $4.9M.
The trick has a price. The crew values the pipeline too little to bother, so the textbook plan holds the pipeline at 25%, the floor. The pipeline is our largest single loss.
This is the trap: the plan only works if we’ve read the crew perfectly.

title: Allocating the Budget
text:
Alignment check
What if the crew wanted what we fear most? We reran the comparison with crew values proportional to our losses. The textbook plan then costs $13.5M, with the crew attacking identity systems. Risk-ranked costs $23.2M, with the crew attacking client data.
The gap does not close. Concentration itself is the problem, not just misreading the attacker: risk-ranked spends heavily on a few assets and leaves the rest cheap to hit, whatever the crew wants.

title: Where Will the Attacker Strike?
text: All money is in $M. Losses are expected loss per targeted ransomware campaign, and the model assumes one campaign per year. All values are illustrative and synthetic.

title: Where Will the Attacker Strike?
text:
The problem
Most security budgets are ranked: list the risks, fund from the top. That treats the attacker as weather. Ransomware crews adapt. They look at what we defend and go where the payoff is best for them.
We study a 500-person fintech firm whose cloud platform is critical infrastructure for its clients. It splits $9.0M a year across six assets, and a ransomware crew picks one to hit. We compare five ways to split the money.

title: Where Will the Attacker Strike?
text:
Three findings

Risk-ranking invites the attack. Funding the top risks first leaves identity at baseline coverage, and the crew goes there. If we read the crew perfectly, expected loss is $13.9M against $7.4M for the robust allocation; if we misjudge it, $13.9M against $9.0M.
The textbook equilibrium looks best on paper and is worst under uncertainty. If we read the crew perfectly, it cuts loss to $4.9M. If we misjudge the crew modestly, the 95th percentile loss is $46.5M.
The robust allocation anticipates the attacker without betting on a perfect read. It cuts expected loss by 35% and the tail by 36% against risk-ranked.



Code
ord <- ms |> arrange(mean) |> pull(strategy)
d <- ms |>
  select(strategy, mean, p95) |>
  left_join(base |> select(strategy, loss_rational), by = "strategy") |>
  mutate(y = match(strategy, rev(ord)))            # numeric row position, best on top
bar_h <- 0.34
ggplot(d) +
  # light bar: crew read perfectly (upper half of each row)
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = loss_rational, ymin = y + 0.02, ymax = y + 0.02 + bar_h,
                fill = strategy), alpha = 0.4) +
  # dark bar: crew misjudged (lower half of each row)
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = mean, ymin = y - 0.02 - bar_h, ymax = y - 0.02,
                fill = strategy)) +
  # whisker from the misjudged mean to the 95th percentile
  geom_segment(aes(x = mean, xend = p95, y = y - 0.02 - bar_h / 2, yend = y - 0.02 - bar_h / 2),
               color = "gray25", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = p95, xend = p95, y = y - 0.02 - bar_h * 0.85, yend = y - 0.02 - bar_h * 0.15),
               color = "gray25", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # labels
  geom_text(aes(x = loss_rational, y = y + 0.02 + bar_h / 2, label = fmt_m(loss_rational)),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4, color = "gray20") +
  geom_text(aes(x = mean, y = y - 0.02 - bar_h / 2, label = fmt_m(mean),
                color = strategy == "uniform"),               # dark text on the pale bar
            hjust = 1.15, size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "gray15", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  geom_text(aes(x = p95, y = y - 0.02 - bar_h / 2, label = paste0("1-in-20: ", fmt_m(p95))),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.1, color = "gray30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = STRAT_COLS, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = d$y, labels = STRAT_LABELS[d$strategy], expand = expansion(add = 0.3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "M"),
                     limits = c(0, max(d$p95) * 1.28), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  labs(x = "Expected loss per campaign", y = NULL,
       title = "Robust wins when we are wrong about the crew",
       subtitle = "Light bar: if we read the crew perfectly.  Dark bar: if we misjudge it (line to the 1-in-20 bad case).") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10))








Figure 1: Expected loss per campaign by strategy, if we read the crew perfectly and if we misjudge it. The line runs to the 1-in-20 bad case.






How to read the plot. For each strategy, the light bar is our loss if we read the crew perfectly; the dark bar is our average loss if we misjudge it, and the line runs to the 1-in-20 bad case.
What the plot tells you. The textbook equilibrium has the lowest light bar and the highest dark bar: it is cheapest on paper and costliest when wrong. The robust strategy gives up some of the paper saving and has the lowest average and the shortest line.







NoteQuestions to ask your CISO




Where does our current plan push an attacker?
Which high-impact assets are we under-protecting because we assume attackers don’t want them?
How would our allocation perform if our threat intelligence is wrong?
What does the next $1M buy under each approach?

title: Where Will the Attacker Strike?
text:
How to read this site

The Game: a two-asset example shows why defending the biggest asset can fail.
Allocation: the firm, the six assets and four ways to split the budget.
Robustness: what happens when we misjudge the crew, and the robust strategy.
Governance: the assumptions, the limits and the automated checks.

title: The Game
text: All money is in $M. Losses are expected loss per targeted ransomware campaign, and the model assumes one campaign per year. All values are illustrative.

title: The Game
section: Why “defend the most valuable asset” fails
text:
Why “defend the most valuable asset” fails
The usual budget logic ranks assets by expected loss and funds the top of the list. That logic treats the attacker as weather: a hazard with fixed odds.
A ransomware crew is not weather. It looks at what we have protected and picks the target that pays best for it. Every dollar we move changes where the crew goes.
So a plan can look careful and still invite the attack. If we protect the crown jewel fully, the crew simply goes next door, and the asset we under-protected takes the hit.

title: The Game
text:
A two-asset example
Take two assets. The production platform (PLAT) would cost us $45M if breached. The identity provider (IDP) would cost $18M. The crew values PLAT at $6M and IDP at $7M, so it slightly prefers IDP. We have one unit of coverage to split between them.
We compare three plans: protect the crown jewel completely, split coverage in proportion to impact, or play the game and equalize what the crew can gain from each target.


Code
g <- two$grid |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(PLAT, IDP), names_to = "target", values_to = "payoff")
plans <- tibble::tibble(
  plan = c("Crown jewel", "Impact-proportional", "Equilibrium"),
  c_PLAT = c(pl$crown_jewel$coverage[["PLAT"]], pl$impact_proportional$coverage[["PLAT"]], pl$equilibrium$coverage[["PLAT"]]),
  loss = c(pl$crown_jewel$loss, pl$impact_proportional$loss, pl$equilibrium$loss)
) |>
  mutate(
    payoff = pmax(
      c_PLAT * a2$A_c[1] + (1 - c_PLAT) * a2$V[1],
      (1 - c_PLAT) * a2$A_c[2] + c_PLAT * a2$V[2]
    ),
    label = paste0(plan, "\nloss ", fmt_m(loss))
  )
ggplot(g, aes(c_PLAT, payoff)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = target, color = target), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = plans, size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = plans, aes(label = label), size = 3.3, min.segment.length = 0,
    nudge_y = c(-2.3, 0.9, -2.8), nudge_x = c(-0.08, -0.02, 0.1), label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(PLAT = "#4D4D4D", IDP = "#7A3E9D"), name = "Crew payoff on") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(PLAT = "solid", IDP = "dashed"), name = "Crew payoff on") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Coverage on PLAT (remainder goes to IDP)", y = "Crew payoff ($M)",
       title = "The equilibrium makes the crew indifferent")








Figure 1: The crew’s payoff on each target as coverage shifts from IDP to PLAT. The equilibrium sits where the lines cross.






How to read the plot. The horizontal axis shows how much of our one unit of protection goes to the platform; the rest goes to identity. Each line is what the crew would earn attacking that target, and it goes wherever its line is higher. Dots mark three plans.
What the plot tells you. Protecting the crown jewel completely leaves identity open, so the crew goes there and we lose most. The equilibrium sits where the lines cross: the crew gains the same either way, and we pick the point that costs us least. Values are made up, so read the shape.



Code
tibble::tibble(
  Plan = c("Protect the crown jewel", "Impact-proportional", "Equilibrium"),
  `Coverage on PLAT` = c(pl$crown_jewel$coverage[["PLAT"]], pl$impact_proportional$coverage[["PLAT"]], pl$equilibrium$coverage[["PLAT"]]),
  `Coverage on IDP` = c(pl$crown_jewel$coverage[["IDP"]], pl$impact_proportional$coverage[["IDP"]], pl$equilibrium$coverage[["IDP"]]),
  `Crew target` = c(pl$crown_jewel$target, pl$impact_proportional$target, pl$equilibrium$target),
  `Defender loss ($M)` = c(pl$crown_jewel$loss, pl$impact_proportional$loss, pl$equilibrium$loss)
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = starts_with("Coverage"), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `Defender loss ($M)`, decimals = 1) |>
  gt_se()




Table 1: Three plans for the two-asset example: coverage, the crew’s chosen target, and our expected loss.

title: The Game
text:
The setup in one paragraph
We choose how much coverage each asset gets. The crew sees our choice and attacks the target with the best payoff for it. We pick the coverage that minimizes our loss given that response. This is a Stackelberg game: we move first, the crew moves second. When the crew is indifferent between targets, we assume it breaks the tie in our favor.






NoteThe math behind the setup





Coverage \(c_t \in [\text{floor},\, c^{max}_t]\) on target \(t\) costs \(k_t c_t\), with \(\sum_t k_t c_t \le B\). Payoffs are
\[U_d(t,c) = c_t U_d^c(t) + (1-c_t)U_d^u(t), \qquad U_a(t,c) = c_t A^c_t + (1-c_t)V_t.\]
The crew picks \(t^* = \arg\max_t U_a(t,c)\). The textbook equilibrium solves one linear program per candidate target and keeps the best for us.

title: The Game
text:
Three assumptions

The crew observes our coverage. It probes before it strikes.
Our commitment is credible. We do not change the allocation after the crew chooses.
We can estimate the crew’s payoffs. This is the weak point. Page 4 relaxes it.

title: Misreading the Attacker
text: All money is in $M. Losses are expected loss per targeted ransomware campaign, and the model assumes one campaign per year. All values are illustrative.

title: Misreading the Attacker
section: Why the textbook answer is fragile
text:
Why the textbook answer is fragile
The textbook equilibrium works by making the crew exactly indifferent across 5 targets. That razor’s edge is what makes the plan efficient, and also what makes it brittle: when the crew’s real payoffs differ from our estimates, the crew steps off the edge toward the target we left weakest.

title: Misreading the Attacker
text:
Misjudged payoffs
We drew 3,000 versions of the crew. In each, every success payoff is multiplied by a random error (lognormal, sigma = 0.35). Every strategy faces the same draws.


Code

hits <- draws |>
  summarise(n = n(), loss = first(loss), .by = c(strategy, target)) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = strategy) |>
  mutate(strategy = factor(strategy, levels = rev(ord)),
         asset = factor(ASSET_SHORT[target], levels = ASSET_SHORT)) |>

callout <- hits |> filter(target == "PIPE", share >= 0.03)   # rare but costly hits

rb_corp  <- share_of("robust", "CORP")

title: Misreading the Attacker
text:
The robust equilibrium
The robust strategy assumes the crew mostly, but not always, picks the best target. It gives each target a chance of being hit that rises with how attractive it is to the crew, then minimizes our expected loss against those chances. A rationality parameter, \(\lambda\), controls how sharp the crew is.
We set \(\lambda =\) 2, chosen on a separate set of simulated crews so the choice is not tuned to the results we report. Optimizing at 2 gives the lowest average loss: $9.13M at 1, $9.03M at 2, $9.83M at 3 and $11.21M at 5.






NoteThe math behind the equilibrium





The crew attacks target \(t\) with probability
\[q_t(c) = \frac{\exp(\lambda U_a(t,c))}{\sum_s \exp(\lambda U_a(s,c))}.\]
We minimize \(f(c) = \sum_t q_t(c)\,\ell_t(c)\) over feasible coverage, with \(\ell_t\) our loss on target \(t\). The gradient is analytic and checked against finite differences. A multistart SLSQP search handles the nonconvexity.

Figure 2: Expected loss against a noisy crew as the crew becomes sharper (higher lambda). Strategies are held fixed.






How to read the plot. The horizontal axis shows how sharp the crew is: low values mean it picks targets almost at random, high values mean it always picks its best one. Each line is a strategy whose coverage is fixed. The vertical axis is our expected loss.
What the plot tells you. The robust strategy has the lowest loss once the crew is moderately sharp (2 is our base case; robust leads from 1 upward). For a nearly random crew, simpler plans do slightly better. The textbook equilibrium is worse than robust at every sharpness.

Figure 3: Expected loss when we misjudge the crew, by budget. The vertical line marks the base budget.






How to read the plot. Each line shows average loss by budget for one strategy when we misjudge the crew. The dotted line is our base budget.
What the plot tells you. Robust is lowest at nearly every budget. Extra money can hurt a simple plan: risk-ranked rises from $12.2M at $11.0M to $15.3M at $14.0M, and textbook from $15.3M at $9.0M to $17.0M at $11.0M, as new coverage pushes the crew toward a thin asset. At $5.5M a baseline edges ahead, though robust still beats the sharp crew it is built for. Above $16.5M every asset hits its cap.

Moving from $9.0M to $10.0M lowers the expected loss from misjudging the crew by $0.83M under robust and $1.55M under risk-ranked. Robust still leads at $10.0M: $8.2M against $12.3M. Across the budget grid from $5.0M to $20M, robust is lowest or tied at every budget except $5.5M.
